extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy of language, and semantics (e.g., undergraduate/graduate philosophy students, logicians, teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Classification and proper use of names in logical analysis: distinguishing concrete vs abstract, connotative vs non-connotative, relative/privative/positive/negative, and modes of application (univocal, equivocal, analogical). Aimed at clarifying signification and avoiding vagueness in philosophical and logical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract vs concrete names (traditional sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'abstract' mean the opposite of 'concrete'; an abstract name is the name of an attribute; a concrete name is the name of an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain the old/schoolman acceptation: do not conflate 'abstract' with all general names. Use 'abstract' to refer specifically to names of attributes (e.g., whiteness = name of color), and 'concrete' for names of objects. The author signals that modern usage has misapplied 'abstract' to many general names and recommends restoring the original distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misappropriate 'abstract' for general names
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the modern practice of applying 'abstract name' to all names resulting from abstraction or generalization (i.e., to all general names); 'abstract' should be confined to names of attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the term 'general name' when referring to names of classes; restore the old usage so the important class 'names of attributes' has a compact distinctive appellation. The author notes that misappropriation 'leaves that important class of words, the names of attributes, without any compact distinctive appellation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary-use/predication determines a word's referent
rubrics_metrics.description: A word ought to be considered as the name of that which we intend to be understood by it when we put it to its principal use, i.e., when we employ it in predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, 'white' in predication (snow is white) is a name of all white objects, whereas 'whiteness' is the name of the attribute. When assessing what a word names, consider its principal predicative use rather than incidental associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative vs non-connotative (absolute) distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-connotative term signifies a subject only, or an attribute only. A connotative term denotes a subject and implies (connotes) an attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to analyze signification: proper names, and pure attribute-names (e.g., whiteness) are non-connotative; adjectives like 'white' are connotative because they denote subjects and connote an attribute. Connotation (what a name implies) is central to a name's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names as non-connotative marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names denote individuals but do not imply or connote attributes; they are essentially marks attached to objects for identification and have, strictly speaking, no signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proper names as labels: their meaning is not derived from attributes (e.g., 'Dartmouth' does not imply location at the Dart's mouth). Use proper names for identification and do not infer attributes from the name itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation (not denotation) carries meaning for connotative names
rubrics_metrics.description: For names that convey information (i.e., have meaning), the meaning resides not in what they denote (the subjects) but in what they connote (the attributes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining or interpreting a connotative name, focus on specifying its connotation (the attributes it implies). Knowing the set of objects a name can be truly predicated of does not suffice to know the name's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix connotation for commonly used general concrete names
rubrics_metrics.description: To alleviate vagueness in language, give every general concrete name which is frequently predicated a definite and fixed connotation so it is clear what attributes are meant when the name is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining an already-used general name, aim to fix connotation with minimal disturbance to the class of objects the name traditionally denotes and with minimal disruption to accepted propositions. This is the purpose of defining connotative names in philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish indeterminate connotation from ambiguity (multiple fixed senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with indeterminate connotation (meaning not precisely fixed) are different from words that have multiple fixed, recognized meanings (ambiguous/æquivocal words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ambiguous words as multiple distinct names that happen to share form; treat indeterminately connotative names as problems requiring fixation of connotation. Avoid conflating the two phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs negative vs privative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names divide into positive (e.g., man, tree, good) and negative (e.g., not-man, not-tree, not-good); privative names denote things that once had an attribute or might have been expected to have it but do not (e.g., blind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that negative-form words may be positive in meaning (e.g., inconvenient = cause of annoyance) and positive-form words may be negative in content (e.g., idle = not working). Privative names connote both absence of certain attributes and presence of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative (non-relative) names and fundamentum relationis
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative names (father, son, cause, effect, like, equal) are always given in pairs and, over and above the object they denote, imply the existence of another object; the attribute they connote is a relation, constituted by a series of facts or events (the 'foundation of the relation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze relative names by identifying the underlying series of events or facts that constitute the relation; recognize that correlative names express the same fact from different perspectives (e.g., 'A is father of B' and 'B is son of A' are equivalent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of employing names: univocal, æquivocal, analogical/metaphorical
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when predicated in the same sense across subjects; æquivocal when predicated in different senses; analogical/metaphorical when predicated in related but not identical senses (a derivative signification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat æquivocal instances as effectively separate names. Use caution with analogical/metaphorical uses: one common fallacy is to argue from the metaphorical use as if it were literal. When analyzing arguments, check whether a term is being used univocally or equivocally.
